<reason>CON (Side A) built a clear distinction from the outset — disclosure of your own price versus compelled steering to a rival channel — and defended it consistently through every precedent PRO offered (airlines, APR, pharmacist). CON's pressure questions extracted two real concessions: PRO admitted no law anywhere compels displaying a rival's price [B4.1], and PRO relocated the "anchor" to the app's own pickup total [B4.3], quietly dropping "independent" from the motion. CON's closing dilemma (pickup toggle = status quo/CON's alternative; "independent" = unverifiable and unworkable) squarely addressed the proposition as written and left PRO defending a narrower motion. CON's restaurant-squeeze argument also went effectively unanswered after PRO's "already happening" response. PRO's core asymmetry framing was appealing and its "novel leverage" reframe was a reasonable move, and its closing landed a real point that CON's all-in pricing fix doesn't surface a side-by-side comparison, but that residual is much smaller than the case PRO opened with ($6-7 gaps against walking in). Both sides had clipped turns, roughly offsetting. CON made the debate easier to decide.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A4.3–A4.4 (with A5.1–A5.5): CON caught PRO's shift between the pressure question and the answer — from grounding a direct-order comparison in menu price to using the app's own pickup total — and showed that this workable version is "the status quo plus a phone number," while reinstating "independent" reintroduces the unverifiable rival-price problem. This turned PRO's strongest late move (the pickup-mode concession) into a concession that the motion as written is either redundant or unworkable.</best_rebuttal>
